title: Dialling 0 on a rotary phone sent ten clicks down the line

cover.alt: Close-up of a telephone's rotary dial with numbered finger holes and a curved metal finger stop.

body: A rotary dial is a pulse generator. You put a finger in a hole, turn the dial clockwise to the finger stop and let go; a spring returns it, a governor keeps the speed steady, and a switch interrupts the line current once per pulse at about **ten pulses per second**. Each digit sent that many pulses, so 1 was one click and 0 was ten, and the exchange counted the clicks to route your call. The first dial installation came with a 99-line automatic exchange in La Porte, Indiana, in 1892, built on Almon Strowger's exchange patent; the familiar finger-hole dial arrived about 1907 and ruled until push-button Touch-Tone phones, first shown at the 1962 World's Fair, took over from the 1960s on.

slides.question: At the standard rate, how many pulses per second did a rotary dial send?
slides.explanation: Ten pulses per second at ordinary telephones, with exchanges usually accepting 9 to 13. Operator consoles often pulsed faster, at 18 per second.

slides.heading: Not everywhere the same
items: Sweden: 0 sent one pulse, 9 sent ten
New Zealand: ten minus the digit, so 7 sent three
Norway used the American way, except Oslo

slides.question: On a New Zealand rotary phone, how many pulses did dialling 7 send?
slides.explanation: New Zealand dials sent ten minus the digit, so 7 produced three pulses. Sweden went the other way, sending one pulse for 0.
